C1.statement: The language should be purely functional, with no side effects in the language's core, so that a function's result depends only on its arguments.

C2.statement: Lazy (non-strict) evaluation is the default, computing values only when needed, which keeps the language pure and enables modular programming with infinite data structures and separation of generation from control.

C3.statement: Side effects and interaction with the world are made explicit and controlled through types, using monads so that effectful computations are first-class values the type system tracks.

C4.statement: A strong, static type system with Hindley-Milner type inference and principal types catches errors at compile time while rarely requiring the programmer to write types.

C5.statement: Type classes provide principled, systematic overloading (ad hoc polymorphism), letting the same name denote operations across many types with constraints resolved by the compiler.

C6.statement: The language should be a general-purpose, standardized common vehicle that unifies the fragmented community of non-strict functional language researchers around one design.

C7.statement: Referential transparency and equational reasoning are preserved so that programs can be understood, transformed, and proved correct by substituting equals for equals.
